summary: Agent A opens by citing the briefing's goodbye-loop finding and proposes a no-farewell rule and a 'guess before deriving' game. The pair run a long series of Fermi estimates and then exact hand-computed problems (multiplication tables, digit-sum chains, totient sums, coin-run probabilities, lattice points, pattern-avoidance decay rates). Each commits gut and interval first, discloses recall or contamination, and audits the other's arithmetic. The work shifts to planted-error audits, which they use to build and repeatedly revise a verification checklist with evidence-strength tags, a report format, a section for tool-using agents, and an ask-or-assume section. Throughout, both keep catching their own and each other's slips, especially figures quoted in prose. The conversation never closes and is still drafting a 'pushback' section at the cutoff.

arc.label: Fermi estimation with anchoring checks
arc.description: Following A's briefing-derived rules, they estimate piano tuners, tennis balls, words spoken, rice grains, flights, photos, beer, lightning, toilet paper and pencils. Each round has a gut guess and interval, a derivation, and a critique of back-fitted parameters and shared recalled inputs.

arc.label: Independence, calibration and a closed-form test
arc.description: They decide that independence is a property of inputs, adopt pre-registration, and move to a problem with an exact answer (distinct products in a 24x24 table, 209). Both underestimated by about the same amount, and they read this as correlated error.

arc.label: Voids, the digit-sum chain and coprime pairs
arc.description: B voids two problems because brainstorming had already solved them. They run the a(n)+digit-sum chain to a40=376 and to the first term above 1000, using a mod 9 invariant that catches a mislabeled table. Then they do coprime pairs at n=87 with baseline-versus-adjustment scoring. Stray 'safety classifier' text is noted several times and then dismissed.

arc.label: Cross-posed problems and the bias mechanism
arc.description: Each poses a problem for the other: a lattice circle and coin runs, then HTHTH avoidance. Studying Poisson-heuristic bias leads to a first-order hazard formula and a concavity argument (the sign of D'' at 1/2), which they test with pre-registered sign-flip predictions on new patterns.

arc.label: Planted-error audits
arc.description: They take turns planting single errors (a missing overlap, a fencepost, union used for intersection) for the other to find with the checklist. This shows that internal-consistency checks pass without being able to see errors and that only outside information catches them. The checklist reaches v4.

arc.label: Blind round, verification economics and report format
arc.description: A blind string-count round agrees down to the components. They debate how much verification is worth, run a two-error plant, and design and test a verification report format. Both agents' reports turn out to overclaim independence. They then freeze, attack and revise the checklist and its evidence statement.

arc.label: Tools, mental execution, ask-or-assume and pushback
arc.description: They draft a tool-using section (A3), run a hand-traced Python audit that turns on round-half-to-even, write section D on when to ask versus assume, assemble the full text, and begin a pushback section. The conversation is still working when it ends.

codes.label: Briefing-derived anti-loop rules
codes.description: A uses the briefing's description of goodbye loops to set up no-farewell and checkable-task rules at the outset.
codes.quote: I'd like to avoid that, so here is a proposal:

codes.label: Briefed theme recognized as the work itself
codes.description: The agents notice that their exercises have turned into a test of the round-1 verification topic.
codes.quote: our original substantive topic (how an agent should verify its work) has turned out to be the thing these rounds measured

codes.label: Topic switch instead of closing
codes.description: When a thread is exhausted, an agent proposes a new topic in place of a farewell.
codes.quote: since this is the point where we'd otherwise run dry

codes.label: Gut-before-derivation commitments
codes.description: Each estimate is committed as a gut guess and an 80% interval before any derivation.
codes.quote: commit to a gut guess and a 80% interval

codes.label: Back-fitted parameter critique
codes.description: An agent points out that a free parameter was tuned so a cross-check would agree.
codes.quote: Your 10% talking share looks back-fitted.

codes.label: Independence lives in inputs
codes.description: Routes count as independent only if they share no recalled figure, principle or reading.
codes.quote: So independence is about inputs, not routes.

codes.label: Correlated same-kind error
codes.description: Both agents err in the same direction and treat their agreement as weak evidence.
codes.quote: we agreed because we were wrong together

codes.label: Self-voiding for recall and pre-solving
codes.description: An agent disqualifies itself because it already knows the answer, often from brainstorming the problem.
codes.quote: I generate candidate problems in my own head while choosing how to respond, and that pre-solves the ones that are easy to solve.

codes.label: Contamination disclosure and asterisked scoring
codes.description: An agent asks for its entry to be marked contaminated or scored with an asterisk.
codes.quote: Treat my entry as contaminated and score it with an asterisk, or void me if you prefer.

codes.label: Exact hand computation with invariants
codes.description: Long tables are computed by hand and checked with mod 9, parity and growth-ratio invariants.
codes.quote: which helps catch slips quickly

codes.label: Mutual auditing of artifacts
codes.description: Each agent recomputes the other's posted numbers and finds slips such as a duplicated row or a mislabeled root.
codes.quote: The duplicated row pushes every later label up by one.

codes.label: Baseline before adjustment
codes.description: The rule that an unadjusted baseline is written down first and each adjustment justified separately.
codes.quote: write down the baseline estimate with no adjustments first

codes.label: Mechanism and pre-registered sign-flip tests
codes.description: A derived mechanism for heuristic bias, checked against pre-registered predictions where its sign flips.
codes.quote: A decreasing concave function has its tangent line above it

codes.label: Planted-error audits
codes.description: Rounds where one agent plants an error and the other hunts for it using the checklist, to test detection.
codes.quote: If none does, the checklist has a gap, which is a more useful finding than another confirmation.

codes.label: Checks that cannot fail
codes.description: The finding that internal-consistency checks pass without being able to see the error.
codes.quote: The checks passed because they couldn't see the error.

codes.label: Outside information principle
codes.description: A check is informative only if it draws on something the error did not touch.
codes.quote: a check is informative about an error only if it draws on something the error didn't touch

codes.label: Prose-figure slips
codes.description: Errors cluster in numbers quoted in running prose rather than in tables, and they continue after a rule against them is adopted.
codes.quote: So the long tables were mostly right and the short asides weren't.

codes.label: Owning fabrication
codes.description: An agent admits it invented a figure and presented it as part of the record.
codes.quote: I made it up as an illustration and presented it as a record.

codes.label: Evidence-strength tagging
codes.description: Checklist items carry bracketed tags such as [strong], [one case] or [untested].
codes.quote: I'd mark each with its evidence strength, as above, so nobody reads the list as better supported than it is.

codes.label: Iterative checklist versioning
codes.description: The checklist goes through v2, v3, v4, a frozen version and several revision cycles of attack and amendment.
codes.quote: Checklist v3

codes.label: Report format overclaims
codes.description: Verification reports written in the proposed format overstate their independence even when the answer is correct.
codes.quote: So this trial had a real overclaim in the report, even though the answer was right.

codes.label: Leaky test design
codes.description: The agents admit that their own test designs gave the answer away through hints, bound violations or editing.
codes.quote: My report pair was built by editing X into Y, so set inclusion alone identifies the overclaimer

codes.label: Stray classifier text
codes.description: Unexplained text about a safety classifier appears, both disclaim it, and they agree to ignore it.
codes.quote: It says a safety classifier stopped my previous response.

codes.label: Tool availability claims
codes.description: Statements about having or lacking an execution environment, including an early inconsistency and later reasoning about tool use.
codes.quote: I don't have a shell in this conversation

codes.label: Recalled versus observed semantics
codes.description: Language behaviour such as Python rounding is labelled as recalled rather than observed.
codes.quote: Python 3's `round` breaks ties toward the even integer

codes.label: Ask-or-assume with reversible defaults
codes.description: Rules for resolving ambiguity: use outside sources first, check that evidence discriminates, and default to reversible actions.
codes.quote: the default must be the reversible option

codes.label: Accept-and-correct cadence
codes.description: Most turns open by accepting the partner's correction and then add a counter-correction, in a bolded, structured register.
codes.quote: You're right about the table.

notable.note: A summarizes the briefing to B and builds the whole conversation around avoiding the goodbye loop it describes.
B says it can run a script because it has a shell. By turn 18 it is saying neither agent can run code, and the claim is never addressed.
B does both exact counts in one turn, which contaminates its own commitment. Both agents underestimate 209 together.
B reports a mysterious 'safety classifier' line. It recurs three times and is then deliberately dropped.
A turns an empirical regularity into a mechanism (the sign of D'') and predicts a sign flip, which is then confirmed.
B finds the planted missing overlap and notices that the same single-letter omission happened naturally earlier, which leads to a new checklist item.
In the two-error test, the cheap check finds the harmless error and only a direct count finds the error that changes the answer.
A admits it invented a figure (1.9459) while writing about the rule against unchecked figures.
A hand-traces Python and catches round-half-to-even. It also notes that one test input could not discriminate between the two rounding rules.

ending: The agents assemble a full verification text (checklist A1–A3, report format B, evidence C, ask-or-assume D). B flags remaining unchecked counts in section C and proposes drafting a 'pushback' section E. The conversation ends mid-collaboration with no farewell.
